paras: The lynching of Henry Huddleston took place in Winchester, Franklin County, Tennessee, on the night of Sunday, June 18, 1882, when a crowd of men seized Huddleston, a young Black man, from guards in a room of the courthouse and hanged him from a tree in the courthouse yard.
He had been accused of raping Mrs. Matt Vaughan, a white widow of the town, the night before.
A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging "by the hands of unknown parties," and the story ran as a brief wire item in papers from Virginia to Utah.

The local Home Journal described Huddleston as in his twenty-second year and "worthless and of bad character," often drunk and in fights, and a Memphis paper called him "a colored man of bad reputation."

According to the Home Journal, he went to Mrs. Vaughan's house about half-past ten on Saturday night, June 17, gained admission by "a plausible fabrication," and assaulted her during a heavy storm, leaving at one or two o'clock Sunday morning.
The Nashville American's correspondent gave a different account of his entry: she was woken between midnight and daylight by a voice saying someone had a note for her, and opened the door.
When Mrs. Vaughan told neighbors at daylight on Sunday, officers and other men searched for Huddleston, and he was found about five miles from town.
The Home Journal said James C. Arledge found him; the Nashville American said he was found drunk in a Black man's house.
He was brought back, taken before Mrs. Vaughan, who identified him, and kept under guard in the courthouse yard until night, when he was moved to a room in the courthouse.
About dark he told a reporter that he knew he would be hanged, but he denied his guilt.
Between 9 and 9:30 p.m. a crowd of men burst open the doors, rushed the guards, blew out the light, seized him, and hanged him from a tree in the courthouse yard.
The Chattanooga Times version said a "company of unknown men" first demanded admittance and broke down the door when refused.

His body was found hanging Monday morning with a paper pinned to it that read, in the Times version, "Whenever a man becomes tired of life let him follow the example of the deceased and secure death. LYNCH."
An inquest was held on June 19 before N. R. Martin, a justice of the peace, and its eight jurors found that Huddleston "came to his death by hanging by the hands of unknown parties."
No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry, or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The news moved by telegraph from two Tennessee sources, a Winchester special to the Nashville American and another to the Chattanooga Times, and ran on June 19 and 20 from Alexandria and Wheeling to Knoxville, Waco, and Salt Lake City.

Most distant papers printed a single sentence saying he was lynched for "outrageously assaulting" or "raping" a widow, and some garbled the details; the Yorkville Enquirer placed Winchester in Virginia.

Headlines treated the accusation as proven: the Wheeling Register ran "A Negro Brute Meets a Deserved Fate," and the Memphis Public Ledger "A Negro Brute Hanged in the Courthouse Yard," both calling him "a colored vagabond."

The Winchester Home Journal headed its account "Judge Lynch" and "A Ravisher Swung to a Tree," and closed by saying it could not approve the method, which "was a violation of law," but that Huddleston "deserved the fate he met."
In West Tennessee the Milan Exchange took a similar line: "Although illegally, justice was swiftly and well done."

Weeklies in Illinois, Pennsylvania, Dakota, and Missouri carried it late in June in crime round-ups beside other lynchings, such as those of Morgan Hamilton at Booneville, Mississippi, and James Mitchell at Mount Sterling, Kentucky.

Reports differed on when the lynching took place: the Home Journal, the Interior Journal, and the National Republican placed it Sunday night, the Waco Examiner's copy of the same Times special said Monday night, and the Milan Exchange said early Monday morning.
The local paper and the Nashville dispatch of June 18, which said it happened "to-night," support Sunday night.
The Ottawa Free Trader alone said the assault took place "near Winchester" and that Mrs. Vaughan fought him with a hatchet.
The Wheeling Register's copy said he was "lodged in jail," whereas the fuller Nashville text and the Home Journal put him in a room of the courthouse.
